newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU states juggle response to Cuba deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU states juggle response to Cuba deal.

text.p: European Union states agreed on Monday to postpone a planned complaint against the U.S. Helms-Burton Act but left until Wednesday more considered reaction to the tentative transatlantic deal on Cuba policy.
"It is agreed that we do not put forward our case in the WTO today," EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told a news conference after meeting with ambassadors from the 15 EU nations.

Brittan said the ambassadors would meet again on Wednesday to decide formally whether to suspend the EU's action against the Helms-Burton Act, which seeks to discourage foreign investment in Cuba, in the World Trade Organisation.

His announcement follows a deal struck between the European Commission and Washington on Friday to defuse a festering row over the Helms-Burton legislation, which aims to isolate the government of Fidel Castro.
The Europeans have been threatening high-profile action at the Geneva-based WTO in retaliation to the U.S. law.

A Spanish diplomat told Reuters that several ambassadors had urged on Monday that the EU hold a strong line against Washington's tendency to enact domestic laws against countries such as Iran, Cuba and Libya without thought to the extra-territorial effects of those laws.

The diplomat said Spain, along with Belgium, France and Italy, had said Wednesday's meeting should prepare a supplementary EU declaration to the deal covering both Helms-Burton and the U.S. Iran-Libya Sanctions Act.
"The EU does not accept extra-territorial legislation. That's something which is not clear in the understanding agreed between with the United States," the diplomat said.
Another element likely to figure on Wednesday is the exact status of the Europeans' WTO complaint about Helms-Burton both while bilateral talks proceed and if they succeed or fail.
"There must be an almost automatic reopening of the panel as a guarantee if the United States takes any action against European companies," the diplomat said.

Under the deal agreed last Friday, the EU would suspend an existing WTO panel and the two sides would negotiate a common policy on properties seized by Cuba's communist government after Castro took power in 1959.

They would also work toward a global agreement on protection of expropriated property. The White House would in exchange seek to change a key provision of Helms-Burton barring executives of companies that invest in disputed properties in Cuba from entering the United States.
Brittan said that talks on the law relating to seized properties should take place in the context of ongoing efforts at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
He stressed that any deal would not apply retroactively to European companies or individuals holding contested property.
Friday's deal included a promise that U.S. President Bill Clinton's six-monthly waiver to parts of Helms-Burton would extend to the end of his administration, he added.
Brittan would not be drawn on the nature of promised "inhibitions" to discourage European countries from buying any more state-seized Cuban property while a deal was being sought.

"Exactly what that should be has not been decided but you could imagine strong inhibitions and weak inhibitions and interim inhibitions. We are not going to announce our negotiating position now," he said.
